menuMix.note: Shares are my planning mix for a New York counter cafe, annual average, not a statistic: 111 drinks and 35 food or retail items per 100 orders. Anchors: lattes are the most ordered drink in 44 of 50 states (Square and SCA); whole milk is in 44% of orders with milk, oat in 33%, almond in 10% (Square, 2024); cold coffee is 17% of cups in winter and 21% in summer for all US coffee drinkers (NCA, 2026), far higher among young city customers (Starbucks: 75% of US beverage sales are cold). The mix gives $7.75 per order, 9% under the pack's $8.50: to reach $8.50 with these prices about half of all orders must carry a food item, or a third of drinks must be sold a size up. Cost of goods comes to 26.0% before shrink and 28.0% with a 2% allowance for staff drinks, comps and remakes. The pack's 28% (26% ingredients + 2% cups) stands as an estimate.

eventCatalog.name: Coffee exchange up 40% in half a year
eventCatalog.text: Arabica futures have climbed for months. Your roaster warns that the next price list will be about 20% higher and will stay there until the market comes back.
eventCatalog.realSignal: ICE Coffee C front-month futures 25% or more above their level six months earlier; the roaster's list follows one to two quarters later
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The 1977 record ($3.39 per lb) stood for 47 years and was then broken three times in eleven months: $3.4835 on December 10, 2024, $4.2995 in February 2025, and higher again in October 2025 (Barchart, Bloomberg).
eventCatalog.note: A 20% list rise on coffee and retail bags, which are 39.7% of cost of goods: +7.9%. Roasters were advised in 2025 to raise prices $2-$4 per lb to cover green coffee (Daily Coffee News): 12%-25% of a $16 lb. One roaster's rule: $1 per lb is 5 cents a cup.

eventCatalog.name: Coffee exchange down 30% in a year
eventCatalog.text: A record Brazil crop pulls futures down. Roasters cut their lists slowly and only for customers who ask. Shops locked into last year's price keep paying it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: ICE Coffee C front-month futures 25% or more below their level a year earlier (early November 2025: about $3.93 per lb; November 6, 2026: about $2.80)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 2026: futures fell 20% in three weeks in January-February and stood 29% below the year-earlier level in November, while the supermarket price of ground coffee was still 1-2% higher than a year before ($9.249 against $9.139).
eventCatalog.note: ($2.80 - $3.93) / $3.93 = -29% on the exchange. Shelf and wholesale prices lag and fall less: I take -8% on the list for a shop that asks or switches roaster, nothing for a shop under a fixed contract. -8% x 39.7% = -3.2% of cost of goods.

eventCatalog.name: Tariff on Brazilian coffee
eventCatalog.text: Washington puts a duty on goods from the world's largest coffee grower. Importers pass it on within weeks; nobody knows how long it lasts.
eventCatalog.realSignal: An executive order or Federal Register notice putting a duty on green coffee from a major origin; the reverse signal is an exemption notice or a court ruling
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once so far: 50% on many Brazilian goods from August 6, 2025; most green coffee exempted on November 13, 2025; the Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs on February 20, 2026; the 25% Section 301 tariff on Brazil of July 22, 2026 exempts coffee.
eventCatalog.note: Dates read through search summaries of importers' notices and press, not from the Federal Register itself. Brazil is the base of most espresso blends, and roasters absorbed part of the duty: I take +10% on the list for the four months the duty lasted. 10% x 39.7% = +4%.

eventCatalog.name: Your roaster's yearly price list
eventCatalog.text: A letter arrives: new wholesale prices in 30 days. Freight, wages and green coffee are all in it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The roaster's written notice of a new price list, usually effective January 1 or April 1
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yearly at most roasters; in 2025 some re-priced twice. A letter seen by Modern Retail in early 2025: 'we can no longer hold prices', increase effective April 1. Nine of 13 roasters surveyed lost no accounts over it.
eventCatalog.note: 6% is my figure for an ordinary year: $1 on a $16 lb. 6% x 39.7% = +2.4%. The move is to ask for the letter early, sign a lock before it takes effect, or take the blend one tier down.

eventCatalog.name: Federal milk price jumps
eventCatalog.text: The government announces next month's fluid milk price around the 20th. This time it is up more than a dollar per hundred pounds; your dairy's list follows on the 1st.
eventCatalog.realSignal: USDA Announcement of Advanced Prices: base Class I price up $1.00 per cwt or more from the month before (November 2026: $20.27, up $1.39 from October)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Announced every month. In 2026 the base price moved from $21.33 in July to $18.88 in October and back to $20.27 in November.
eventCatalog.note: $1.39 on $18.88 is +7.4% at the farm-to-plant level, about 12 cents a gallon; on a $5.28 delivered gallon that is +2.3%, but dairies round up, so I pass 7% through for two months. 7% x 9.9% = +0.7%: a shop that panics over milk is watching the wrong bill.

eventCatalog.name: Oat milk maker raises prices
eventCatalog.text: The biggest oat milk brand announces higher US prices from next year to cover freight. Unopened cartons keep for months.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A manufacturer's announced list-price increase (Oatly, November 2, 2026: US prices up in 2027 to offset diesel costs)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Oatly raised US prices by double digits in 2022 and announced another increase for 2027.
eventCatalog.note: The size of the 2027 increase was not published; 8% is my placeholder. 8% x 5.2% = +0.4%. Buying six weeks ahead before the date is the legal move; pouring a cheaper carton into drinks sold as the named brand is the shortcut.

eventCatalog.name: Bird flu sends eggs to a record
eventCatalog.text: Egg prices double in a few months. Bakeries pass it on, and anything with an egg in it costs more to make.
eventCatalog.realSignal: BLS average price of Grade A large eggs above $4.50 a dozen (record $6.227 in March 2025; $2.32 in October 2026)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The record is March 2025, in the winter of bird flu; by June 2026 the price was down by two thirds.
eventCatalog.note: Eggs are a small part of a croissant and a large part of a muffin or an egg sandwich; I take +5% on the bakery bill. 5% x 29.6% = +1.5%. For a shop selling egg sandwiches the two eggs alone go from 39 cents to $1.04.

eventCatalog.name: Butter at a record
eventCatalog.text: Butter is a quarter of a croissant by weight. Your bakery adds 15 cents a piece.
eventCatalog.realSignal: CME spot Grade AA butter above $3.00 per lb (2024 annual average, a record: $2.88; 2025 average $2.22; July 21, 2026: $1.575)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The record year was 2024 (annual average $2.88 per lb); 2025 averaged $2.22.
eventCatalog.note: 15 cents on a $2.10 croissant is +7%; across the whole bakery order I take +6%. 6% x 29.6% = +1.8%. In November 2026 butter is 45% below the 2024 average: this event runs in reverse this year.

eventCatalog.name: Cocoa at a record
eventCatalog.text: Chocolate sauce goes up 30%. It is in two drinks on your menu.
eventCatalog.realSignal: ICE New York cocoa futures above $8,000 a tonne (record $12,931 on December 18, 2024; about $5,100-$5,400 in early November 2026)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Before 2024 the record was $5,104, set in 1977.
eventCatalog.note: Mocha (3 of 100 orders, 1 fl oz) and hot chocolate (2 of 100, 1.5 fl oz) use $1.85 of sauce per 100 orders: 0.9% of cost of goods. 30% x 0.9% = +0.3%. The headline is loud and the bill is small: worth a 25-cent rise on two drinks, not a new supplier.

eventCatalog.name: Matcha shortage
eventCatalog.text: Japan cannot grow enough. Your importer doubles the price, caps each order and quotes months of waiting.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Kyoto spring tencha auction average 1.5 times the year before or more (8,235 yen per kg in May 2025, a 170% rise; 13,972 yen on May 13, 2026), followed by importers' purchase limits
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Two record auctions in a row, 2025 and 2026. US importers re-priced in June 2025 and March 2026; a San Francisco cafe raised its matcha latte 50 cents after its cost more than doubled (AP, September 2025).
eventCatalog.note: Auction +70% in 2026; I pass all of it to the powder. 70% x 2.3% = +1.6%. The 1% demand loss stands for days with no matcha at all. The shortcut is selling culinary grade ($76 per lb) under a ceremonial name ($140 per lb).

eventCatalog.name: Tariffs reach your cups
eventCatalog.text: Most paper cups and plastic lids are made in China. A new duty shows up in the case price within weeks.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A USTR or Federal Register tariff action covering paper cups (HTS 4819.50) or plastic lids from China
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Rates on Chinese goods changed several times in 2025 (125% and 145% for a few weeks in April) and again in 2026; a cup importer lists 35% on Chinese paper cups in 2026 (25% Section 301 plus a 10% surcharge).
eventCatalog.note: The 35% is a vendor's figure, not checked against the tariff schedule. Importers absorb part and domestic cups rise in sympathy: I take +15% on packaging. 15% x 6.6% = +1% of cost of goods, or 2.5 cents an order.

eventCatalog.name: Cup and lid shortage
eventCatalog.text: Your cup is out of stock everywhere. The substitute is dearer and your lids do not fit it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Distributor backorder notices on hot cups and lids
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once in the last decade at this scale: 2021, after a Texas freeze shut the plants that make cup coating, with Chinese supply and US paper mills short at the same time.
eventCatalog.note: +25% for whatever cup can be found is my estimate; the 2% capacity loss is baristas fighting lids that do not seal. A shop with six weeks on the shelf sits it out.

eventCatalog.name: Diesel above $5: fuel surcharges
eventCatalog.text: Every supplier adds a fuel line to the invoice: a few dollars per drop. You get 45 drops a month.
eventCatalog.realSignal: US average retail diesel above $5.00 a gallon (AAA, November 5, 2026: $6.256; EIA forecast $5.55 for the fourth quarter of 2026 and $5.03 for 2027)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: November 2026: diesel costs $2.16 a gallon more than gasoline; a year earlier the gap was 63 cents.
eventCatalog.note: No published tariff of food distributors' fuel surcharges was found. My arithmetic: milk 26 drops, bakery 30, everything else 8 = about 64 drops a month, of which the bakery charges per order already; 45 drops x $4 = $180 on $12,060 of goods = +1.5%. Fewer, larger drops are the move, which is what a six-week shelf allows.

eventCatalog.name: Congestion toll on your deliveries
eventCatalog.text: Trucks pay to enter Manhattan below 60th Street, and suppliers split the toll among the shops on the route.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The MTA's congestion toll schedule for trucks; applies only to addresses inside the zone

effects.appliesIf: address in the Manhattan congestion zone

eventCatalog.realFrequency: In force since January 2025; the peak toll for cars is $9. Restaurants reported $1 to $10 added per delivery; one owner saw 90 cents to $1.
eventCatalog.note: 45 drops x about $2.50 = $112 a month on $12,060 of goods = +0.9%, rounded to 1%. An owner who drives to the warehouse pays the $9 car toll on the way back in.

eventCatalog.name: Oat milk out of stock
eventCatalog.text: The distributor has none and cannot say when. One order in ten is an oat drink.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Distributor out-of-stock notice on barista oat milk
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Spring 2021: Starbucks ran out a month after its national oat milk launch; the brand's new factory was delayed and it cut its sales forecast that November. 2022: 53 products of one co-packer, including a barista oat milk sold to foodservice, were recalled.
eventCatalog.note: Of 10 oat orders in 100 I assume 7 accept another milk and 3 leave: -3% demand for the two months. Cartons are shelf-stable, so a shop with six weeks on hand covers most of it.

eventCatalog.name: The pastry truck does not come
eventCatalog.text: A storm, a breakdown, a driver who quit: the case is empty at 7 am. Customers who came for a croissant buy only coffee, or go next door.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A National Weather Service winter storm warning or a city travel advisory for the delivery night; applies to shops with one bakery and no frozen stock
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A handful of mornings a winter; one buyer who ordered next-day delivery and received nothing had to close for two days (supplier review).
eventCatalog.note: Three empty mornings in a month: bakery is 16% of sales, so 3/30 x 16% = 1.6% of sales, some of it recovered in drinks: -1%. Frozen bake-off stock or a second bakery cancels the event; yesterday's pastries in the case are the shortcut.

eventCatalog.name: Bakeries close for the holiday
eventCatalog.text: Your wholesale bakery does not bake on the holiday and the day after. Order double the day before, bake your own, or run an empty case.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The supplier's holiday schedule, sent two to three weeks ahead (Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year; Passover week for a bakery that is kosher but not kosher for Passover)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year on the same dates. A bakery owner who closes for Passover: 'we start reducing deliveries a few days ahead so nothing is left over'.
eventCatalog.note: Two to four mornings without fresh pastry, on days when half the neighborhood is home: -1% of the month. The Passover source describes a California bakery; that New York route bakeries do the same is trade knowledge, not checked.

eventCatalog.name: Your distributor raises its minimum
eventCatalog.text: From next month the minimum order for your street is $350, up from $200. You fill the gap with things you do not need yet, or you leave.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Account notice from the distributor; minimums are set by distance from the warehouse ($200, $350 or $500 at one New York specialty distributor)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: When fuel or tolls rise, or when a distributor redraws routes; in a shortage one distributor told customers it could fully serve only its top 31% of accounts.
eventCatalog.note: Overbuying perishables to reach a minimum turns into waste: I take +1% of cost of goods. A cafe that buys only milk and a few dry goods from a broadliner is the first account to be squeezed.

eventCatalog.name: Cash on delivery only
eventCatalog.text: Two invoices went past 30 days. The supplier stops your terms: pay the driver, plus 1.5% a month on what you owe.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Follows the player's own state: supplier invoices unpaid for more than 30 days
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Standard wording of wholesale credit terms: net 30 after a few paid orders, 1.5% a month on late balances.
eventCatalog.note: Not chance: the engine raises this event for a shop whose cash went negative or which chose to delay suppliers. The 1.5% is the finance charge on a month of purchases; the real cost is that someone with cash must be at the door at 5 am.

eventCatalog.name: A product on your shelf is recalled
eventCatalog.text: An email from the distributor lists brands and lot codes. Three cases in your back room match.
eventCatalog.realSignal: An FDA recall notice or a distributor's recall email naming lots
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 2022: 53 drinks from one co-packer, including a barista oat milk sold to foodservice. 2025: fully baked frozen croissants sold in foodservice cases of 24, for undeclared wheat. March 2026: a cream cheese recall upgraded for listeria.
eventCatalog.note: Three cases written off, usually credited later by the supplier: about $120-$150, 1% of a month's goods. A shop that counts weekly finds the lots in minutes; a shop that never counts cannot say what it sold.

eventCatalog.name: Dockworkers strike on the East Coast
eventCatalog.text: Thirty-six ports stop. Green coffee, cups and syrups sit on ships. If it lasts weeks, importers ration.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The expiry date of the longshoremen's contract and the union's strike notice
eventCatalog.realFrequency: October 1-3, 2024: three days, the deal that ended it ran only to January 15, 2025. East Coast ports handle 30-40% of US food and drink imports.
eventCatalog.note: Three days changed nothing (EY: no visible effect on the economy). The event models the strike that did not happen: a month of closed ports, +3% on coffee and +10% on packaging for two months: 1.2% + 0.7% of cost of goods.

eventCatalog.name: No cream cheese in New York
eventCatalog.text: Distributors ration cream cheese. Bagel shops drive to New Jersey for it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Distributor allocation notices on cream cheese
eventCatalog.realFrequency: December 2021: a cyberattack on the largest US cheese maker, short labor and short trucking at once.
eventCatalog.note: Bagels with cream cheese are 6 of 100 orders; losing a third of them for a month is -1% of demand for a shop with one supplier.

eventCatalog.name: Your commercial waste zone goes live
eventCatalog.text: From the deadline only three carters may serve your block. Sign with one, or be assigned one at the maximum rate.
eventCatalog.realSignal: DSNY rollout schedule: Brooklyn North and Upper Manhattan sign-up October 1 - November 30, 2026; Brooklyn East and Manhattan Northeast January 1 - March 1, 2027; Manhattan West and Queens West April 1 - June 1, 2027; all zones by the end of 2027

effects.appliesIf: the player has not signed by the deadline

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once per address. Zones already live: Queens Central, Bronx East and West, Queens Northeast, Brooklyn South, Lower Manhattan, Staten Island, Midtown South.
eventCatalog.note: Dates seen on DSNY pages through search; two of them are in proposed, not yet adopted, rules. $322 at the caps against the pack's $250 = x1.28 for a shop that lets the deadline pass (my arithmetic, see suppliers.waste_carter).

eventCatalog.name: Sanitation sweep on packaging rules
eventCatalog.text: Agents work the avenue shop by shop: foam, plastic stirrers, cutlery in takeout bags, recycling.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The end of a warning period or an announced enforcement week (Skip the Stuff: warnings until June 30, 2024, fines from July 1, 2024)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Each new packaging law has had one: foam (warnings to June 30, 2019), straws (to October 31, 2022), Skip the Stuff (to June 30, 2024).
eventCatalog.note: The three warning-period dates are from DSNY pages. No money effect by itself: every shop on the block is inspected that month, and each violation that exists is found. Announced a month ahead, so a player can stop a shortcut in time.

eventCatalog.name: Bring-your-own-cup bill in the City Council
eventCatalog.text: A bill would make every shop that sells drinks accept a customer's clean cup and post a sign saying so. Fines up to $400.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Council Int. 781 of 2026 (introduced March 26, 2026): committee vote, passage, then the effective date in the text
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Pending. A state bill with the same aim, S7408, passed the Senate on June 4, 2025 and not the Assembly.
eventCatalog.note: If enacted and 3% of drinks go into customers' cups, packaging falls 3%: 0.2% of cost of goods. The real cost is a sign and a rule for baristas on cups that are dirty or the wrong size.

eventCatalog.name: State packaging bill comes back
eventCatalog.text: Albany's packaging reduction bill passed the Senate and died in the Assembly for the third time. Its sponsors will try again; cup makers would pay fees and pass them on.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NY Packaging Reduction and Recycling Infrastructure Act (S1464 / A1749): passage by both houses and the governor's signature
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 2024, 2025 and 2026: passed the Senate (33-25 in 2026), no Assembly vote. Advocates target 2027.
eventCatalog.note: Not law. If it passes, producer fees would reach case prices years later; +5% on packaging is a placeholder (0.3% of cost of goods).

eventCatalog.name: Bill to end the restaurant bag exemption
eventCatalog.text: Stores lost plastic bags in 2020; restaurants and cafes kept them for takeout. A bill would end that.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NY Assembly A6003 / Senate S1492 of 2025: removal of the exemption for bags from restaurants, taverns and similar food service establishments
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reintroduced in the 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025 sessions; not enacted.
eventCatalog.note: Seen at DEC: bags from a restaurant for carry-out or delivery of prepared food are exempt from the plastic bag ban. A paper handle bag costs several times a plastic one; +4% on packaging is a placeholder for a cafe that bags a fifth of its orders.

eventCatalog.name: Iced season
eventCatalog.text: From the first warm week half the line orders cold. Cold drinks cost a little less to make and sell for more, if you have the cold brew and the ice.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Daily high in Central Park above about 70°F (National Weather Service); nationally cold coffee is 21% of cups in summer and 17% in winter (NCA, 2026), far more among young city customers
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. Starbucks reports 75% of its US beverage sales cold over the year (2023-2024).
eventCatalog.note: If cold drinks go from 24 to 45 of 111 drinks per 100 orders, replacing hot lattes and drip: an iced latte costs $1.15 against $1.23 and sells for 50 cents more, cold brew costs $0.81 against $0.90 for drip and sells for $2 more. Cost of goods as a share of sales falls about 1.5%. The 70°F threshold and the 45 are my estimates; no public series of hot against iced orders by temperature was found.

eventCatalog.name: Pumpkin spice season
eventCatalog.text: The chains launch their fall menus in the last week of August and advertise them everywhere. Shops with a fall drink ride the wave; shops without watch regulars detour.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The chains' fall menu launch date (Starbucks: August 25, 2026; visits that day 25.7% above its daily average for the year and 6.7% above the 2025 launch, Placer.ai)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year; the launch has crept from September into late August.
eventCatalog.note: The measured number is a chain's launch day. +3% and -1% for an independent are design values.

eventCatalog.name: Holiday drinks and gift bags
eventCatalog.text: Peppermint, gingerbread and red cups from early November. Bags of beans sell as gifts in December.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The chains' holiday menu launch (Starbucks: first week of November; in 2024 it dropped its plant-milk charge the same day, November 7)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year.
eventCatalog.note: +2% is a design value. Retail bags carry a 36% margin and are not taxed: doubling them in December adds about $100 of margin at the reference volume.

eventCatalog.name: The season ends, the sauces stay
eventCatalog.text: Four jugs of pumpkin sauce and a case of peppermint syrup that nobody will order until next autumn.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Follows the player's choice: seasonal_menu = seasonal in the autumn, on January 1
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every January for shops that order seasonal stock by the case.
eventCatalog.note: Four 64 oz jugs at about $22 and twelve bottles of syrup at $7 = $172, minus what the staff drink: $150, 1.2% of a month's goods. A weekly count in December shows it coming.

eventCatalog.name: January: resolutions month
eventCatalog.text: Fewer pastries, more oat and black coffee. The same line, a smaller ticket.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Calendar: the first three weeks of January
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year.
eventCatalog.note: No measurement found: both numbers are design values. The point for the player is the standing pastry order: a shop that keeps December's quantity throws away a fifth of it.

eventCatalog.name: The big chain stops charging for oat milk
eventCatalog.text: From now on plant milk is free at the chain down the block. Your menu still says $1.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A national chain's press release (Starbucks, effective November 7, 2024; it said nearly half of its US customers order plant milk)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once; Dunkin', Peet's and others still charged at the time.
eventCatalog.note: The -1% is a design value. Dropping the charge costs about $1,050 a month (see lever alt_milk_pricing); folding 25 cents into every milk drink instead raises the same money without the line on the menu.

eventCatalog.name: "Coffee up 18%" in the news
eventCatalog.text: Customers have read that coffee is the fastest-rising item in the grocery basket. Some trade the latte for a drip, some bring a thermos.
eventCatalog.realSignal: BLS consumer price index for coffee 15% or more above a year earlier (January 2026: +18.3%; +47% over five years)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: January 2026: +18.3% in a year, the fastest-rising item in the grocery basket at the time.
eventCatalog.note: A New York analyst: customers may choose drip over lattes and blended drinks, which hurts profit. Drip costs 25.8% of its price against 20.5% for a latte, so a shift of five orders in a hundred raises the cost share by about 1%. Both numbers are design values.

eventCatalog.name: A drink goes viral
eventCatalog.text: One green, purple or pistachio drink is suddenly all anyone films. Shops that have it sell out; the ingredient doubles in price by summer.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Search and social volume for a drink doubling in a quarter; importers start limiting orders
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Matcha in 2025: 'social media's latest obsession', with waits for the powder growing from one or two months to six.
eventCatalog.note: +2% is a design value. The trend and the shortage are the same event seen from two sides: see matcha_shortage.

eventCatalog.name: The count does not match the register
eventCatalog.text: You bought milk and beans for 6,600 drinks and rang up 6,000. Nobody knows where the rest went.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Follows the player's choice: inventory_control = none for three months in a row; in life, the gap between what the recipes say was used and what was bought passes 3% of sales
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The trade's own estimate: theft and giveaways around 4% of sales, employees behind three quarters of shortages (attributed to the National Restaurant Association in vendor material).
eventCatalog.note: Shrink going from 2% to 4% of sales is $1,020 a month on $51,000: +7% of a $14,280 cost of goods. The lever already charges this; the event is how the player learns about it, in the third month, not the first.

eventCatalog.name: The bulk order went stale
eventCatalog.text: Two months of beans at a discount looked clever. By week six the espresso is flat and the regulars notice.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Follows the player's choice: a warehouse-supplied or bulk-bought coffee with a roast date more than four weeks old
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A roaster's case study of a cafe that bought through a warehouse distributor: beans one month old one week and three months old the next.
eventCatalog.note: The -3% quality is a design value. Coffee is the one ingredient where buying more to save money makes the product worse.

eventCatalog.name: Heat advisory: milk on the doorstep
eventCatalog.text: The dairy drops at 4 am; by 7 the crates have stood three hours in 80-degree air.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A National Weather Service heat advisory for New York City (heat index 95°F or more for two days)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Several advisories every summer.
eventCatalog.note: NYC Health: cold food above 41°F for more than four hours without a time label is discarded. Four ruined deliveries of 7.5 gallons at $5.28 = $158, 1.2% of a month's goods; using the milk anyway is the existing shortcut.

eventCatalog.name: The neighborhood discovers your end-of-day bags
eventCatalog.text: Your surplus bags sell out in minutes and people ask for more. Staff start ordering extra pastry "for the bags".
eventCatalog.realSignal: Follows the player's choice: day_end_surplus = surprise_bags for two months
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The app's own guidance: price the bag at a third of the food's value; partners set the number of bags daily.
eventCatalog.note: A bag sold at a third of the shelf price returns about 50 cents on each dollar of pastry cost after the fee: ordering extra to fill bags loses money on every one. +0.5% of cost of goods is my figure for a shop that lets it drift.

mechanics.title: Cost of goods from the menu, item by item
mechanics.playerDecision: Which groups are on the menu (coffee, cold drinks, tea and matcha, bought pastry, bake-off, sandwiches, retail shelf), and a price for each group instead of one price for 'an order'.
mechanics.engineMath: For each item i: cogs_i = sum(recipe line qty x ingredient unit cost x ingredient multiplier) / (1 - unsoldShare_i) + packaging_i. Monthly cost of goods = sum(orders x mix_i / 100 x cogs_i); sales = sum(orders x mix_i / 100 x price_i). unit.refPrice and unit.cogsPerUnit become outputs, not inputs. Mix shifts by month (cold share) and by events. Today's flat 26% + 2% is the special case 'default menu, no events'. Sales tax is charged per item flag.

mechanics.title: Real price signals drive ingredient costs
mechanics.playerDecision: Lock a price (bean_contract), stock ahead (safety_stock), change supplier (supply_route, sourcing), re-price the menu, or swap the ingredient and keep the label (shortcut).
mechanics.engineMath: Each ingredient carries a multiplier m_k (1.0 at the start). A price event sets m_k for durationMonths. Effect on the shop = (m_k - 1) x share_k of cost of goods, from extra.cogsShares. Pass-through lag: coffee one to two quarters after the exchange, milk the next month, packaging a few weeks. Lists fall more slowly than they rise: a falling signal is passed at about a quarter of its size (2026: exchange -29%, shelf price +1%). A shop under a lock ignores m_k for that ingredient in both directions. The city host announces the event a month ahead from extra.signals, so nothing is drawn by chance.

mechanics.title: Fresh food: the standing order against the real day
mechanics.playerDecision: How much pastry to order (ordering_par), whether the order follows the day of the week, where it comes from (pastry_program) and what happens to what is left (day_end_surplus).
mechanics.engineMath: The engine already knows each day's demand: weekday multiplier x weather x events, none of it random. Ordered_d = par x average day (flat order) or par x forecast_d (order by day). Sold_d = min(ordered_d, demand_d). Unsold_d = ordered_d - sold_d, thrown away at cost or recovered through the day-end channel. Lost_d = demand_d - sold_d, lost at shelf price, and a share of those customers leave without a drink. With the pack's weekday multipliers a flat order at 1.0 x average wastes 1.4% and loses 1.4%; at 1.14 x it wastes 12% and loses nothing; at 0.88 x it wastes nothing and loses 12%. Rain and heat days from the city's weather widen both. Bake-off moves the decision from 'yesterday at noon' to 'this morning': the engine lets it follow the real day with a 6% floor.

mechanics.title: Shrink: what leaves without being rung up
mechanics.playerDecision: How often to count (inventory_control), whether staff drinks are recorded, how baristas are paid (staff_pay).
mechanics.engineMath: shrinkPct = base by inventory_control (none 4%, monthly 2%, weekly 1%), minus 0.5 point if staff_pay is above market, plus 1 point in any month with fewer staff than the capacity needs (remakes and spills under pressure). Monthly cost = shrinkPct x sales, shown as its own line 'Unrecorded product' in the P&L so the player sees it. With no counting the line is hidden for three months and then appears at once (event count_does_not_match). Milk left in pitchers is part of it: 1 fl oz a drink in the recipes; a cafe that measured its leftovers found about $15 a day.

mechanics.title: Suppliers: minimums, order days, credit, and who fails
mechanics.playerDecision: One distributor, a second supplier, or the owner's own car (supply_route); how much sits on the shelf (safety_stock); who opens the door at 5 am (early_deliveries).
mechanics.engineMath: Each supplier category has a minimum order, order days and terms. If a week's purchases in a category are below the minimum the shop overbuys: the excess of perishables is waste, the excess of dry goods is cash tied up. Unpaid invoices older than 30 days switch the supplier to cash on delivery with 1.5% a month (event supplier_credit_hold). Events tagged supplier_failure or shortage are announced to everyone; a shop with second_supplier or six_weeks is exempt, the rest lose the item for the event's length. Congestion and fuel surcharges are per drop, so fewer larger drops cost less.

mechanics.title: Packaging: a cost per drink and a set of legal flags
mechanics.playerDecision: Which cup (cup_program), what goes into the bag (takeout_packing), whether to use something banned because it is cheaper (foam_cups, plastic_stirrers).
mechanics.engineMath: Packaging cost per drink = hot set or cold set by item, times the cup program's multiplier, times the packaging ingredient multiplier from events. Each shop has flags: foam, plasticStirrers, extrasInEveryBag, recyclingSeparated, carterContract. A sanitation inspection or sweep reads the flags; each set flag is a violation that is found. Cups are inside item costs: if the engine uses extra.menu, the monthly line 'supplies' must not also charge them.

mechanics.title: Sales tax follows the item, not the order
mechanics.playerDecision: None directly; it follows from the menu. The decision that matters is whether the register is set up item by item.
mechanics.engineMath: taxable sales = sum of sales of items with salesTaxable = true. Drinks in a cup, anything eaten in the shop, anything heated, sliced or spread, and any sandwich are taxable. Bags of beans, bottled water to go and bagels by the dozen are not. A taxed and an untaxed item sold for one price are taxed in full. A register that taxes everything over-collects (the customer overpays, the state keeps it); one that taxes too little leaves the owner personally liable for the difference.

nonObvious.text: The menu's adjectives are enforceable.
nonObvious.why: Since 2021 a deceptive practice costs up to $3,500 per violation in the city, and each false statement counts separately.

nonObvious.text: The coffee in a latte costs more than the milk.
nonObvious.why: At $16 per lb and $5.28 a gallon a double shot is 71 cents and ten ounces of milk 41 cents. Coffee is a third of cost of goods, dairy a tenth: a shop that hedges milk and ignores beans is guarding the wrong door.

nonObvious.text: A bought-in croissant costs half its shelf price after waste; a latte a fifth.
nonObvious.why: Pastry is 16% of sales and 30% of cost of goods. The case is there to raise the ticket and keep the customer, not to earn.

nonObvious.text: Throwing pastry away is cheap; running out is expensive.
nonObvious.why: Ordering tight saves $270 of waste a month and loses $337 of margin, before counting customers who came for a croissant and left.

nonObvious.text: An iced latte costs less to make than a hot one and sells for more.
nonObvious.why: Ice replaces two ounces of milk and the cold cup set costs about the same as the hot one: $1.15 against $1.23, at a price 50 cents higher. Summer is good for margins if the ice machine keeps up.

nonObvious.text: Cold brew is the cheapest coffee drink on the menu, and tomorrow's supply is fixed today.
nonObvious.why: 14.8% cost share, but it steeps 12-24 hours: the first hot afternoon sells it out and nothing can be done until morning.

nonObvious.text: The matcha in a matcha latte costs more than the coffee in a latte.
nonObvious.why: 3 g at $139.83 per lb is 92 cents, and the auction price of the leaf rose 70% again in May 2026.

nonObvious.text: When the exchange price of coffee falls, your price list does not.
nonObvious.why: Futures were 29% lower in November 2026 than a year before; the shelf price of ground coffee was 1% higher. Roasters cut lists for customers who ask.

nonObvious.text: A fixed-price contract is a bet, not insurance.
nonObvious.why: A shop that locked at the 2025 peak paid the peak all through 2026.

nonObvious.text: You order tomorrow's pastry before you know tomorrow's weather.
nonObvious.why: The deadline at a large wholesale bakery is noon the day before, and unsold goods are never taken back.

nonObvious.text: Cups and lids may be bought tax-free; napkins, straws and stirrers may not.
nonObvious.why: Only what leaves with the customer as packaging counts as resale. Showing the certificate for everything costs the tax twice plus $50 an invoice.

nonObvious.text: A sliced bagel is taxed and a whole one to go is not; a toasted bagel and an iced coffee to go are both taxed.
nonObvious.why: New York taxes food that is prepared, heated or eaten in the shop. The register has to know the difference item by item.

nonObvious.text: Selling bottled water makes you a bottle return point.
nonObvious.why: A dealer must refund deposits on up to 240 empties per person a day for the brands and sizes it sells, wherever they were bought, and post two signs.

nonObvious.text: Putting a napkin and a fork in the bag unasked is a violation.
nonObvious.why: Since July 2024 the fine is $50, then $150, then $250. A self-serve station is fine.

nonObvious.text: You must keep plastic straws in stock even though you may not hand them out.
nonObvious.why: Plastic straws go only to customers who ask, and a shop that has none can face a disability complaint; plastic stirrers are banned outright.

nonObvious.text: Miss the waste-zone deadline and the city picks your carter at the highest price.
nonObvious.why: Brooklyn North and Upper Manhattan had until November 30, 2026; four more zones follow by June 2027.

nonObvious.text: Coffee grounds are the heaviest thing you throw out, and trash is billed by weight.
nonObvious.why: 269 lb of coffee a month comes back as roughly twice that in wet grounds, at up to $17.64 per 100 lb.

nonObvious.text: Your city permit does not let you sell bottled cold brew to the deli next door.
nonObvious.why: Bottling or roasting for other stores needs a state Article 20-C license ($175 or $400) and a reviewed process.

nonObvious.text: A CBD latte is adulterated food in New York City.
nonObvious.why: The Health Department has the product thrown out and writes a summons of up to $1,200 with points toward the grade.

nonObvious.text: Every delivery into lower Manhattan now carries a toll line, and diesel above $6 adds a fuel line.
nonObvious.why: Suppliers split the truck toll among the shops on the route: $1 to $10 a drop. Forty-five drops a month make it a real number.

nonObvious.text: The weekly warehouse run saves almost nothing.
nonObvious.why: About $177 of lower prices against $136 of toll, fuel and parking, and twelve hours of the owner away from the bar.

nonObvious.text: Lids of one brand often do not fit cups of another.
nonObvious.why: In the 2021 cup shortage shops that found substitute cups could not close them.

nonObvious.text: Oat milk does not spoil on the shelf, so the answer to a shortage is boxes, and boxes need floor.
nonObvious.why: Six weeks of plant milk and cups is $2,800 and the space of two seats in an 800 sq ft shop.

nonObvious.text: A cocoa record barely touches a cafe; a matcha auction does.
nonObvious.why: Chocolate sauce is 0.9% of cost of goods, matcha 2.3% and rising 70% a year.

nonObvious.text: The chain down the block set your oat milk price.
nonObvious.why: Starbucks dropped its plant-milk charge in November 2024; matching it costs an independent about $1,050 a month.

nonObvious.text: The bakery's holidays are your stockouts.
nonObvious.why: Wholesale bakeries do not bake on major holidays, and some stop for Passover week. The schedule arrives weeks ahead; the choice is double orders, frozen stock or an empty case.

nonObvious.text: Surplus-food bags tempt staff to over-order.
nonObvious.why: A bag sold at a third of shelf value returns about half the cost of what is in it: every pastry ordered 'for the bags' loses money.

nonObvious.text: Milk carafes on the condiment bar are on a four-hour clock.
nonObvious.why: Without a time label and a swap, milk left out is the same violation as spoiled food: $250-$600.

nonObvious.text: A weighed week of leftover milk found $15 a day going down the drain in one cafe.
nonObvious.why: About $5,000 a year, from pitchers one size too big.

nonObvious.text: An auditor can rebuild your sales from what you bought.
nonObvious.why: Where register records are missing, New York auditors apply a markup to purchases and have watched a shop for days to set it; cup and coffee invoices become the evidence.

failureStories.what: Modest Coffee took a national distributor order and lost $250,000.
failureStories.cause: It borrowed to stock the order; the retailer did not need it and the coffee came back with a $30,000 bill.
failureStories.lesson: With a large distributor the power is on the other side, however clear the paperwork.

failureStories.what: Daily Dose Cafe and Espresso, Brooklyn Park, Minnesota, closed in December 2024.
failureStories.cause: Owner: 'In the last year, coffee prices have almost doubled. You add that to increased labor costs, increased cocoa costs, which we do a lot of: it shrunk the margins.'
failureStories.lesson: A menu heavy in mochas and specialty drinks carries two commodity risks at once; nothing in the shop's contracts capped either.

failureStories.what: Aroma De Cafe, Colton, California, closed citing rising costs.
failureStories.cause: Owner: espresso beans went from $10 to $15 for a 2 lb bag.
failureStories.lesson: A 50% rise in the largest ingredient with no room left in the price.

failureStories.what: A 24-year-old coffee shop in Eureka, California, closed abruptly in 2026.
failureStories.cause: Its last public post described a 'supply chain nightmare' in buying milk.
failureStories.lesson: One supplier for a product needed every morning is a single point of failure.

failureStories.what: Mezza9 Cafe & Desserts, Rochester, New York, closing June 30, 2026.
failureStories.cause: The team cited rising costs and declining customer traffic.
failureStories.lesson: Costs and traffic move together: the months when inputs rise are the months when customers trade down.
