officials.name: Sanitation enforcement agent
officials.realProcess: Agents walk commercial blocks and write a Notice of Violation on the spot: for trash put out wrong, recyclables in the garbage, shop trash in a corner basket, foam cups on the counter. Repeat notices inside 12 months cost more each time. Fines are argued at the city's hearings office (OATH), not in court.

violations.name: Foam cups or containers
violations.law: NYC Admin Code §16-329 (Local Law 142 of 2013); NY Environmental Conservation Law Art. 27 Title 30, §71-2730
violations.note: DSNY's page for businesses: $150 for the first offense, $250 for the second and $500 for the third and later, per Notice of Violation inside 12 months; the city ban has been enforced since July 1, 2019. The text of Local Law 142 itself says $250, $500 and $1,000, and the state law (in force January 1, 2022) says up to $250, $500 and $1,000 in a calendar year: I use the lower schedule the department publishes. Game formula: $150 in the first month, $250 in the second, capped at $500. A shop with under $500,000 of yearly income can ask for a 12-month hardship waiver instead.

violations.name: Plastic stirrers, or plastic straws handed out unasked
violations.note: Seen on DSNY and NYC311 pages: since November 1, 2021 food businesses may not give out plastic stirrers or splash sticks at all, plastic straws only on request, and must keep plastic straws in stock for anyone who asks; fines per Notice of Violation inside 12 months, enforced since November 1, 2022 by DSNY, the Health Department and DCWP. The amounts ($100, $200, $400) are from the law's text and the Council committee report, not from the DSNY page. A 2023-2024 small-business relief law (Local Law 151) removed part of the straw paperwork; I could not confirm which parts, hence estimate. Game formula: $100, $200, $300, capped at $400.

violations.name: Utensils, napkins and packets put in takeout bags unasked
violations.law: NYC Admin Code §16-402 (Local Law 17 of 2023, 'Skip the Stuff')
violations.note: DSNY's page: $50 for a first violation, $150 for a second and $250 for a third and later inside 12 months; in effect since July 31, 2023, warnings until June 30, 2024, fines since July 1, 2024. Covers utensils, condiment packets, napkins and extra containers in takeout and delivery orders; a self-serve station inside the shop is allowed. For orders that come through a delivery app, relying on what the app says the customer asked for is a complete defense. Game formula: $50 a month of violation up to $250, a little gentler than the real ladder.

violations.name: No contract with an authorized private carter
violations.law: NYC Admin Code §16-116; Title 16-B (Commercial Waste Zones, Local Law 199 of 2019)
violations.note: Seen in DSNY's printed summary of rules (2015): $100 for not having a private carter under §16-116(b). DSNY's 2025 Commercial Waste Zone report calls the penalties under §16-116 'relatively low' and asks the Council to raise them, so $100 is the floor, not a 2026 schedule. In a zone that has gone live a business with no contract is assigned a carter at the zone's maximum rate: that is why the game formula adds back everything saved.

violations.name: Shop trash in a public litter basket
violations.note: DSNY's litter basket page: misusing a public basket can be fined up to $350; baskets are not for household or commercial waste. DSNY's printed summary of rules (2015) gives the ladder for storekeepers: $100, then $250, then $350. Agents open bags and read the cups and receipts inside. Game formula: $100 in the first month, $175 in the second, capped at $350.

violations.name: Recyclables thrown out with the trash
violations.note: DSNY's set-out rules page for businesses: $100 for the first offense, $200 for the second, $400 for the third and later. Every business must recycle; a food business separates metal, glass, plastic, cartons, foil and cardboard from trash. A cafe throws out a lot of cardboard (milk and cup cases) and milk jugs. Food scraps: only shops of 7,000 sq ft or more, or chains with two or more city locations totalling 8,000 sq ft, must separate them, so a single small cafe is exempt.

violations.name: Resale certificate used for things you do not resell
violations.criminal: Issuing a false or fraudulent resale certificate with intent to evade tax can be prosecuted as a felony, and the state can revoke the Certificate of Authority, which shuts the register.
violations.note: NY Tax Department penalty bulletin and Form ST-120: misuse costs $50 for each document plus 100% of the tax due, on top of the tax itself. The restaurant purchases bulletin draws the line: cups, lids, carry-out bags, sleeves, plates and wrappers go to the customer with the food and may be bought tax-free with Form ST-120; napkins, straws, stirrers and plastic utensils, cleaning supplies and equipment may not. Game formula: the unpaid tax back, the same amount again, and $50 for each month's invoice.

violations.name: CBD or another banned additive in drinks
violations.law: NYC Health Code §71.05, §81.07; NY Cannabis Law (cannabinoid hemp retail license)
violations.note: NYC Health guidance 'Adulterated Foods': cannabinoids such as CBD are adulterants; a food service establishment may not make or offer food or drink with CBD or cannabis; the inspector has the product thrown out, writes a summons with points toward the letter grade, and can close a shop that repeats. The department's workshop slide gives a penalty of up to $1,200. A shop may sell sealed CBD products only with a state cannabinoid hemp retailer license. The split into $400 plus $200 a month is my game formula; only the $1,200 ceiling was seen.

violations.name: Menu says organic, single-origin or oat; the cup holds something cheaper
violations.law: NYC Admin Code §20-700, §20-703 (Consumer Protection Law, as amended by Local Law 98 of 2021); NY General Business Law §349
violations.note: DCWP: Local Law 98 of 2021 raised the top fine for unfair trade practices seven-fold, from $500 to $3,500 per violation; each false statement is its own violation, and a knowing violation is $3,500. The department's penalty schedule for §20-700 lists $525, $1,050 and $3,500 (search summary of the rule text; I could not read which column is the first offense). Serving dairy to a customer who paid for oat is also an allergy hazard. Game formula: $525 in the first month, $1,050 in the second, capped at $3,500.

violations.name: Recalled product kept on sale
violations.law: NYC Health Code §71.05 (adulterated or misbranded food), §81.07; 21 U.S.C. §331
violations.criminal: Knowingly selling adulterated food that injures someone can be prosecuted under the federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
violations.note: NYC Health's guidance on adulterated food: the inspector has the product discarded and writes a summons with points toward the letter grade; the department's workshop slide gives a penalty of up to $1,200, and repeated violations can close the shop. A recall-specific line of the penalty schedule was not found; the $600 start is my game formula. The reputation hit stands for the news story, not the fine.

shortcuts.name: Buy foam cups from an out-of-state seller
shortcuts.what: Foam cups run about 2 cents less than paper ones, roughly $100 a month at 200 orders a day. Single-use foam has been banned in the city since 2019 and in the state since 2022: $150, then $250, then $500 per notice.

shortcuts.name: Plastic stirrers and a straw in every cold cup
shortcuts.what: Plastic stirrers and unwrapped plastic straws are the cheapest on the shelf and save a few seconds per drink: about $40 a month. Plastic stirrers are banned and plastic straws are on request only: $100, then $200, then $400.

shortcuts.name: Cancel the private carter and take the trash home
shortcuts.what: No carter contract: about $250 a month saved. Every business must have an authorized private carter; the city does not collect business trash, and in a waste zone you get assigned a carter at the maximum rate anyway.

shortcuts.name: Feed the corner litter basket
shortcuts.what: Pay the carter for fewer pickups and push the overflow into the city's corner baskets: about $80 a month. Agents open the bags and find your cups: $100, then $250, then $350.

shortcuts.name: One bag for everything
shortcuts.what: No sorting, no second bin, no cardboard to flatten: about $40 a month of staff time and service. Every business must separate recyclables: $100, then $200, then $400.

shortcuts.name: Buy everything tax-free on the resale certificate
shortcuts.what: Show the resale certificate for napkins, stirrers, cleaning chemicals and small equipment as well as cups: about $55 a month of sales tax not paid. An audit bills the tax, the same amount again as a penalty, and $50 per invoice.

shortcuts.name: Sell CBD lattes
shortcuts.what: A CBD shot for $3 extra brings in about 1% more sales. The Health Department treats CBD in food or drink as adulteration: the product is thrown out, the summons can reach $1,200, and the points count toward your letter grade.

shortcuts.name: Keep the premium words, pour the cheap stuff
shortcuts.what: The menu still says single-origin, organic milk and Oatly; the bar pours a commodity blend and the cheapest cartons. Saves about 3% of sales. Each false claim is a separate deceptive practice: $525 and up, $3,500 if you knew.

shortcuts.name: Keep selling a recalled product
shortcuts.what: The recall notice names lots that are on your shelf. Pulling them means a write-off of about $150 and a day without the item. Selling recalled food is selling adulterated food: a summons of up to $1,200, and a lawsuit if anyone gets sick.

reports.name: Report trash, recycling or banned packaging (311)
reports.text: The Sanitation Department sends an agent to look at the curb, the bins and the cups on the counter. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a false menu claim or a banned additive (311)
reports.text: Consumer protection or the Health Department checks what is really in the cup against what the menu says. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

ruleCards.title: No foam
ruleCards.text: Single-use foam cups, clamshells, plates and trays are banned in the city (since 2019) and the state (since 2022). Fines run $150, $250, then $500 per notice in 12 months. A shop under $500,000 a year can ask for a one-year hardship waiver.

ruleCards.title: Straws and stirrers
ruleCards.text: Plastic stirrers and splash sticks: banned since November 2021; use wood. Plastic straws: only when a customer asks, and you must keep some in stock for people who need one. Fines $100, $200, then $400.

ruleCards.title: Skip the Stuff
ruleCards.text: For takeout and delivery, no utensils, napkins, condiment packets or extra containers unless the customer asks. A self-serve station in the shop is fine. Fines since July 1, 2024: $50, $150, then $250.

ruleCards.title: You must hire a carter
ruleCards.text: The city does not pick up business trash. In a live waste zone you choose among three authorized carters; miss the sign-up deadline and you are assigned one at the maximum rate. Citywide caps: $26.87 per cubic yard or $17.64 per 100 lb.

ruleCards.title: Corner baskets are not yours
ruleCards.text: Public litter baskets are for pedestrians. Shop trash in a basket costs up to $350 a time, and agents open bags to see whose cups are inside.

ruleCards.title: Business recycling
ruleCards.text: Every business must recycle. A cafe separates metal, glass, plastic, cartons and cardboard from trash: $100, $200, then $400. Food scraps must be separated only by shops of 7,000 sq ft or chains; one small cafe is exempt.

ruleCards.title: Bins with lids, after 8 pm
ruleCards.text: Since March 1, 2024 every business puts trash out in bins with secure lids, not loose bags: one hour before closing or after 8 pm, back inside before you reopen. Fines start at $50-$100 and reach $200-$400.

ruleCards.title: What you can buy tax-free
ruleCards.text: Cups, lids, sleeves, bags and wrappers go home with the customer: buy them tax-free with a resale certificate. Napkins, straws, stirrers, utensils, cleaning supplies and equipment are taxed. Misuse costs 100% of the tax plus $50 a document.

ruleCards.title: The sliced bagel rule
ruleCards.text: A dozen bagels to take away: no sales tax. A plain bagel eaten in the shop, or one toasted or with cream cheese even to go: 8.875%. Any sandwich is taxed. Sell a taxed and an untaxed item for one price and the whole price is taxed.

ruleCards.title: The 5-cent bottle
ruleCards.text: Sell bottled water or soda and you charge a 5-cent deposit, post two signs and take back empties of the brands and sizes you sell: at least 240 per person a day, in all open hours except the first and last.

ruleCards.title: No CBD in the cup
ruleCards.text: The Health Department treats CBD and cannabis in food or drink as adulteration. The product is thrown out, the summons can reach $1,200 and the points count toward your grade. Sealed CBD goods need a state retail license.

ruleCards.title: The menu is a promise
ruleCards.text: Organic, single-origin, local, oat: every word on the menu must be true of what is in the cup. Each false claim is a separate deceptive practice; fines were raised in 2021 from $500 to as much as $3,500 per violation.

ruleCards.title: Milk on the counter
ruleCards.text: Cold food may sit out without refrigeration for up to 4 hours only if it carries a label with the time it came out and the time to throw it away. After that it is discarded, never put back in the fridge.

ruleCards.title: Bottling for other shops
ruleCards.text: Your city permit covers what you sell at your own counter. Bottling cold brew or roasting coffee to sell to other stores needs a state Article 20-C food processing license: $175 a year for a small independent, $400 otherwise.

ruleCards.title: When a product is recalled
ruleCards.text: A recall names brands, sizes and lot codes. Check your shelves the same day, pull what matches, keep the supplier's credit note. Food under recall is adulterated food: a summons of up to $1,200 and points toward your grade.

levers.name: Pastry

options.label: Baked pastries delivered before opening
Bake frozen pastry in the shop through the morning
Hire a baker and bake from scratch
Drinks only, no food

levers.note: At the reference month (6,000 orders): 780 croissants, 420 muffins, 300 cookies and 360 bagels sold, $3,564 of bakery bought, $394 of it thrown away. Bake-off: a delivered croissant costs $2.43 per one sold after 12% waste, a frozen ready-to-bake one $1.50 after 6% waste (price seen at WebstaurantStore), so croissants alone save $725 a month; muffin batter and cookie dough are assumed to save another $600 (not checked). Against that: 45 minutes of staff time a day ($420 a month with payroll taxes) and about $80 of electricity and parchment. Net about -$900. Scratch baking: ingredients fall to about a quarter of the shelf price (saves about $1,400 on $8,400 of bakery sales) but a baker at $22 an hour for 120 hours costs $2,900 with payroll taxes: net +$1,500, and it needs a kitchen the notes' format does not have. A negative monthlyCost is a saving. 'Drinks only' removes about 16% of sales (bakery is $1.40 of a $7.75 order); the engine has no field for ticket size, so it is written as -5% demand.

levers.name: Oat and almond milk

options.label: $1 extra for plant milk
Plant milk at no extra charge
Dairy only

levers.note: Oat milk costs 10.4 cents an ounce against 4.1 for dairy (both seen): 63 cents more per 12 oz latte. With the upcharge, 10 of 100 orders are oat drinks. Without it I assume oat rises to a third of milk drinks (Square, 2024: oat is in 33% of orders with milk), 22 of 100 orders: 600 lost upcharges ($600) plus 720 more oat drinks at 63 cents ($454) = $1,050 a month at 6,000 orders. Starbucks dropped its 70-80 cent charge on November 7, 2024 and said nearly half of its US customers order plant milk, so a customer now meets the charge mostly at independents. Dairy only: no cartons to waste (-$150) but every tenth order walks.

levers.name: Unsold food at closing

options.label: Throw it away
Sell it in surprise bags through a surplus-food app
Donate it to a food rescue group
Staff take it home

levers.note: About 223 unsold items a month with a shelf value of $900. Too Good To Go: the shop packs surplus into a bag priced at a third of its value ($300 a month) and pays an annual fee plus a fee per bag; the only US figure found is 'about 25%' (2023 press), so $225 is kept. Payouts come quarterly. Donation: the federal Good Samaritan Food Donation Act shields a good-faith donor from liability unless grossly negligent, and Internal Revenue Code §170(e)(3) gives an enhanced deduction; the money value of the deduction is left out. The fourth real option, selling it tomorrow, is the existing shortcut keep_old_food.

levers.name: How much fresh food to order

options.label: Enough for a normal day: about one in eight left over
Order to sell out by mid-afternoon
A full case until closing

levers.note: Standard: 12% of bakery unsold (trade guide: 10-15%), $394 a month at cost. Tight: 4% unsold saves $270, but an empty case after 2 pm loses about 8% of $8,415 bakery sales: $673 of sales, $337 of margin. The saving and the loss are nearly equal, which is the lesson: wasted pastry is cheap, a missed sale is not. Abundant: 22% unsold, $894 thrown away, $500 more than standard. Demand effects are design values.

levers.name: Coffee price

options.label: Pay the roaster's current price list
Lock today's price for 12 months against a volume commitment

levers.note: The reference shop buys about 269 lb of coffee a month ($4,150), a third of its cost of goods. A lock is free to sign and cuts both ways: someone who locked in late 2025, with the exchange near $3.90 a lb, was still paying that level in November 2026 with the exchange at $2.80. Roasters themselves buy forward; whether a given roaster will hold a price for a small cafe is a matter of negotiation, not a published tariff. Engine: while the lock runs, coffee events in either direction do not touch this shop.

levers.name: How supplies reach the shop

options.label: One cafe distributor delivers overnight
Owner drives to the cash-and-carry warehouse every week
Keep a second supplier on every key item

levers.note: Dry goods, plant milk and disposables are about $2,200 a month at the reference volume. Cash-and-carry: I assume 8% cheaper ($177) against four trips at about $34 each for the $9 congestion toll, fuel and parking ($136): the trip saves almost nothing in cash and costs the owner 12 hours a month off the floor. Second supplier: split orders lose volume discounts and meet two minimums; $120 is my estimate. In exchange, events tagged supplier_failure do not empty the shelves.

levers.name: Counting stock

options.label: Count once a month
Weekly count against the register, recipes in the POS
Order by eye, never count

levers.note: Shrink (free drinks for friends, unrecorded staff drinks, remakes, over-pouring, product that walks out the back) is taken as 2% of sales with a monthly count, 1% with a weekly count and 4% with none. On $51,000 of sales: weekly saves $510 and costs $260 of a shift lead's time, net -$250; no counting costs $1,020 more. The 4% is the figure the trade repeats and attributes to the National Restaurant Association (theft about 4% of sales, employees behind about 75% of inventory shortages); I found it only in vendor blogs, so all three levels are estimates.

levers.name: Cups

options.label: Plain stock cups
Custom-printed cups with your logo
Compostable cups and lids

levers.note: About 6,660 cups a month. Compostable: the hot cup alone is 8.2 cents against 4.6 (both seen), and I take 4.5 cents more per set: $300. Custom print: about 4 cents more per cup at small runs (my estimate): $265. Printers' terms seen: one case of 500-1,000 with 3-4 weeks' lead time at one supplier; 50 cases and 14-19 weeks at another; 30,000 paper cups and 12 weeks at a third. A sticker or stamp on a stock cup is the cheap version. Compostable cups in New York end up in the trash unless the carter collects organics.

levers.name: Napkins, stirrers and cutlery

options.label: Only when the customer asks; self-serve station in the shop
Staff drop a set into every bag

levers.note: The old habit is faster at the register and costs about 1.5 cents an order in napkins and cutlery nobody asked for ($90 at 6,000 orders, my estimate). Since July 2024 it is a violation for takeout and delivery orders.

levers.name: Seasonal drinks

options.label: Same menu all year
A seasonal special every quarter

levers.note: $250 a month for sauces, toppings, a menu reprint and the unsold seasonal stock written off when the season ends (my estimate). The 3% is a design value; the only measured figure is for a chain with national advertising: Starbucks visits on its fall launch day, August 25, 2026, were 25.7% above its daily average for the year (Placer.ai). A seasonal latte sells for $1.25 more than a plain one with 34 cents of extra ingredients.

levers.name: Milk for drip coffee

options.label: Staff add milk behind the counter
Self-serve carafes, time-labelled and swapped every 4 hours
Carafes sit on the bar from open to close

levers.note: NYC Health: cold food may be held without temperature control for 4 hours if labelled with the time it came out and the time to discard it, and must then be thrown away. Three swaps a day waste about a pint of milk and half-and-half each: 36 cents a pint x 3 x 30 = $32, plus labels: $45 (my arithmetic). Carafes left out all day are the existing violation spoiled_food ($250-$600).

levers.name: Shelf-stable stock on hand

options.label: One week of cups, plant milk, syrups and matcha
Six weeks on the shelf

levers.note: Dry goods, plant milk and disposables run about $2,200 a month at the reference volume, so five extra weeks is about $2,800 of cash sitting in boxes: 24 cases of oat milk, 8 cases of cups, lids and sleeves. $60 a month covers shelving and the odd case that goes out of date (my estimate). The catch is space: in 800 sq ft the boxes take the place of two seats or a staff corner. Events tagged shortage do not empty the shelves of a shop that holds six weeks.

levers.name: Deliveries before opening

options.label: Someone comes in an hour early to receive and check
Drivers have a key and a code and stock the fridge
Crates are left at the door

levers.note: Milk and pastry arrive between 3 am and 7 am. An extra paid hour a day at $17 plus payroll taxes is $580 a month. A key drop costs nothing but nobody checks temperatures, counts or dates at the door (the small quality loss is a design value). Crates on the sidewalk warm above 41°F on any mild morning and are sometimes gone by opening: that is the existing violation spoiled_food.

levers.name: Trash pickup

options.label: Ask all three zone carters and sign the cheapest
Miss the deadline and take the assigned carter at the maximum rate
Three pickups a week instead of six

levers.note: The pack budgets $250 a month. At the caps a shop putting out 40 lb a day pays about $322 in a $110-a-month zone (see suppliers.waste_carter), so 'assigned at the maximum' is about $70 above a negotiated contract. Fewer pickups save part of the frequency charge (my estimate $60) and leave food waste in the shop for two days: smell and pest pressure, written as a small quality loss.

levers.name: Cold brew

options.label: A measured batch every evening for tomorrow
Big batches twice a week, always in stock

levers.note: Cold brew steeps 12 to 24 hours, so tomorrow's supply is decided today. A measured daily batch runs out on the first hot afternoon; big batches never run out but about one batch in ten is poured away when it passes its week (12 servings x 81 cents x 4.5 = $45 a month, my arithmetic). In the iced season the event iced_season penalises the daily batch.

setup.name: Countertop convection oven for bake-off pastry
setup.note: WebstaurantStore: Avantco CO-28M half-size electric countertop convection oven, 208/240 V, $459.99. Range on the same page family: Galaxy $329.99 (120 V), Waring WCO500X $859.00, steam-injection models $1,000-$2,500, Moffat turbofan above $5,000. A 208/240 V oven needs its own circuit; ask the Fire Department and your architect whether your model needs a hood. Lifespan is my estimate for a light-duty unit.

setup.name: One-section reach-in freezer for frozen pastry
setup.note: WebstaurantStore: True T-12F-HC 25-inch one-section reach-in freezer $3,653.60. Budget Galaxy GRI-18-FW $1,199.00 (rated 1 of 5 by buyers); scratch-and-dent True T-19FZ-HC $2,584.00; Beverage-Air FB27HC 30-inch $5,415.65. A case of 80 croissants is about a week of sales at the reference volume. Lifespan is my estimate.

monthlyCosts.name: Cups, lids, sleeves, napkins, bags
monthlyCosts.note: Kept at $0.17; now built bottom-up. Seen at WebstaurantStore: hot set 11.1 cents (12 oz cup $45.99 per 1,000, lid $30.49 per 1,000, sleeve $41.49 per 1,200), cold set 10.4 cents (16 oz PET cup $59.49, strawless lid $44.49 per 1,000). With 111 drinks and 35 food items per 100 orders the packaging that leaves with the customer is 13.3 cents an order; napkins, wooden stirrers, sugar and straws on request add about 3.5 cents (my estimate). If the engine starts costing the menu item by item (extra.menu), cups are already inside each item's cogs: drop this line then, or it is counted twice.

events.name: Wholesale coffee up 20%
events.text: Your roaster's new price list passes on higher green coffee prices. Beans are about a third of what an order costs you to make.
events.note: Correction of the existing event. Share: in the costed menu (extra.menu) coffee is 34% of cost of goods, not 25%: 20% x 34% = +6.8%. Size: the BLS shelf price of ground coffee was $9.139 per lb in September 2025 and $9.332 in September 2026 after peaking at $9.72 in April 2026; the exchange price doubled between late 2023 and February 2025 ($4.2995 per lb). A 2025 trade advisory told roasters that $2-$4 more per lb would cover the rise in green coffee: on a $16 lb that is 12%-25%. Duration: roasters buy months ahead, so a new list stays for two quarters, not one.

events.name: Milk up 10%
events.text: Your dairy distributor re-prices from the monthly federal milk price. Milk goes into most of the drinks you sell, but it is a smaller bill than the coffee.
events.note: Correction of the existing event. Share: in the costed menu dairy milk is 9.9% of cost of goods (226 gallons, about $1,200 a month), not 30%: 10% x 9.9% = +1%. With oat milk the whole 'milk' line is 15%. Size: the federal Class I base price went from $18.88 per cwt in October 2026 to $20.27 in November (+7.4% in one month); the shelf price moved between $4.026 and $4.317 a gallon inside 2026 (7%).

roadmap.title: Cost every item before you print the menu
roadmap.text: Write the recipe of each drink in grams and ounces, price each line from a supplier quote, add the cup and lid, and add what you expect to throw away. A latte should cost you about a fifth of its price; a bought-in croissant about half.

roadmap.title: Open supplier accounts and file your resale certificate
roadmap.text: Each supplier wants a credit application, often with a personal guarantee, and your Certificate of Authority number. New accounts usually pay on delivery for the first orders. Give Form ST-120 only for goods that leave with the customer: cups, lids, bags.

roadmap.title: Check packaging and trash rules for your address
roadmap.text: No foam, no plastic stirrers, straws and cutlery only on request. Find your commercial waste zone and its sign-up deadline, pick one of the three carters, and buy lidded bins before the first night.

suppliers.what: Wholesale roasted beans in 5 lb bags, usually with barista training and equipment service included
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the cafes you like who roasts for them, then visit two or three roasters for a cupping. Ask each for the price list, the minimum, the roast day and what happens to the price when the market moves.
suppliers.examples: Partners Coffee, Joe Coffee Company, Brooklyn Roasting Company, Variety Coffee Roasters, Devocion, Counter Culture Coffee
suppliers.priceAnchor: $11.75-$17.20 per lb in 5 lb bags; typical tiers $12 per lb at 10-25 lb a week, $11 at 26-50 lb
suppliers.minimumOrder: From none to 15 lb per order or 40 lb a month, depending on the roaster
suppliers.paymentTerms: Net 15 to net 30 once you have a history; the first orders are prepaid; late balances carry about 1.5% a month
suppliers.leadTime: Roasted to order once or twice a week, delivered within two days; a missed order day means a week on old beans or a walk to a competitor's shelf
suppliers.failureModes: A new price list on 30 days' notice; a blend reformulated when an origin gets too dear; beans from a warehouse distributor arriving one to three months off roast
suppliers.monthlyVolume: About 269 lb at 6,000 orders a month
suppliers.note: Correction of the existing entry: terms added. Seen through search: Joe Coffee 5 lb Waverly blend $80 on Faire ($16.00 per lb); Atomic $17.20 per lb (research notes); Dilworth $11.75 and $15.25 per lb; Klatch minimum 15 lb an order; Kean 40 lb a month in 5 lb bags; Methodical no minimum; a trade guide: cafes order 5-25 lb a week at $10-$15 per lb, tiers $12 and $11, terms net 15-30; a green coffee importer: net 30 after three orders, 1.5% a month on late balances; a roaster's own case study on warehouse beans one to three months old. Roaster names are well-known examples, not endorsements.

suppliers.what: Whole milk by the gallon, half-and-half and cream, delivered two to six mornings a week
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the neighboring cafes which dairy truck already stops on your block: a route that passes your door is cheaper than one that detours. Ask who owns the crates and what an unreturned crate costs.
suppliers.examples: Dairy routes run by regional processors and by specialty distributors such as Baldor or Dairyland (The Chefs' Warehouse); Restaurant Depot for emergencies
suppliers.priceAnchor: About $5.28 a gallon delivered (national restaurant invoice average); $4.10 on the supermarket shelf in October 2026
suppliers.minimumOrder: A specialty distributor out of the Bronx: $200, $350 or $500 an order by distance, no delivery fee; a milk route: a few crates per stop
suppliers.paymentTerms: Weekly statement or cash on delivery for new accounts
suppliers.leadTime: Order by evening for the next morning; drops land between 3 am and 7 am, often before anyone is in the shop
suppliers.failureModes: Crates left on the sidewalk warm up or walk away; a short-dated delivery leaves you three days to use it; the price list moves every month with the federal Class I price; a storm or a holiday skips your day
suppliers.monthlyVolume: About 226 gallons at 6,000 orders a month: two crates a day
suppliers.note: Correction of the existing entry: terms added. Seen through search: Baldor's help center gives order minimums of $200, $350 or $500 for accounts served from the Bronx warehouse depending on distance and no delivery fee for business accounts; Toast's invoice data gives $5.28 a gallon for whole milk (year not stated). Delivery hours and crate practice are trade knowledge, not a published tariff.

suppliers.what: Croissants, muffins, cookies and bread baked overnight by a licensed wholesale bakery and delivered before opening
suppliers.whereToFind: Wholesale programs of local bakeries: ask for the wholesale menu, the minimum, the order deadline and the days they do not bake. Ask whether they credit anything for damaged goods; nobody credits unsold ones.
suppliers.examples: Balthazar Bakery, Bien Cuit, Ceci-Cela, Colson Patisserie, Pain d'Avignon, Orwashers, Amy's Bread
suppliers.priceAnchor: About $2.10 for a butter croissant that sells for $4.75 (roughly half of the shelf price)
suppliers.minimumOrder: $30 an order in Manhattan and $40 elsewhere at one large bakery, plus about $1 per delivery
suppliers.paymentTerms: Weekly invoice; standing order by day of the week
suppliers.leadTime: Changes until about noon the day before; delivered every night of the year the bakery bakes
suppliers.failureModes: You order tomorrow's pastry before you know tomorrow's weather; no returns of unsold goods; bakeries close on major holidays, and a bakery that is kosher but not kosher for Passover may stop for the week
suppliers.note: Correction of the existing entry: terms added. Balthazar Bakery's wholesale FAQ: minimum order $30 in Manhattan, $40 everywhere else; baguette orders until noon the day before delivery; delivery every night to Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and parts of New Jersey, Westchester and Rockland. Its wholesale menus of 2020 list a $1.00 delivery charge. The croissant price is my estimate (see extra.ingredients). Other names are well-known examples from general knowledge, not checked.

suppliers.what: Cups, lids, sleeves, bags, wooden stirrers, napkins, straws kept for those who ask
suppliers.whereToFind: Order online by the case, or carry cases out of a cash-and-carry warehouse. Before you order a pallet, check that the lid fits the cup: lids of one brand often do not fit cups of another.
suppliers.examples: WebstaurantStore, Restaurant Depot, Imperial Dade, Odeko
suppliers.priceAnchor: Hot set 11.1 cents (12 oz cup, lid, sleeve); cold set 10.4 cents (16 oz cup, strawless lid); compostable hot cup 8.2 cents alone
suppliers.minimumOrder: One case of 1,000; free shipping needs a $99 a month membership and $29 of eligible goods per order
suppliers.leadTime: Two to five days by parcel; a case of 1,000 cups is the size of a filing cabinet drawer, and a week of cups for a busy shop is seven of them
suppliers.failureModes: The exact cup goes out of stock and the substitute needs different lids; tariffs on imported cups land in the price with a few weeks' lag; storage is the real limit in 800 sq ft
suppliers.monthlyVolume: About 6,660 cups at 6,000 orders a month
suppliers.note: Correction of the existing entry: terms added. WebstaurantStore: WebstaurantPlus costs $99 a month ($49 for each extra address) and gives free shipping on orders with at least $29 of eligible items; cup, lid and sleeve prices are in extra.ingredients. The lid-fit problem was the lesson of the 2021 cup shortage (Wall Street Journal via trade press).

suppliers.what: Private carter for trash and recycling: a monthly charge by pickup frequency plus a charge by weight or volume
suppliers.whereToFind: The Sanitation Department lists the three carters authorized for your commercial waste zone and each one's maximum price. The maximum is a ceiling: ask all three for a quote below it.
suppliers.examples: The three carters authorized for your commercial waste zone
suppliers.priceAnchor: Citywide cap outside live zones: $26.87 per cubic yard or $17.64 per 100 lb. In zones: a monthly charge for five pickups a week of at most $110 (Brooklyn North, Queens Central, Queens Northeast, Queens West) to $353 (Manhattan Southeast), plus the weight charge
suppliers.minimumOrder: A written service agreement; the monthly frequency charge is due even in a slow month
suppliers.leadTime: Sign before your zone's deadline (Brooklyn North and Upper Manhattan: November 30, 2026) or be assigned a carter at the maximum rate
suppliers.failureModes: A missed pickup leaves your bins on the sidewalk past opening, which is your violation, not the carter's; coffee grounds are heavy and you pay by weight
suppliers.note: Correction of the existing entry: prices added. Business Integrity Commission: maximum $26.87 per cubic yard of loose refuse or $17.64 per 100 lb. City Comptroller's review of the zone contracts: the monthly maximum for five-day service runs from $110 to $353 by zone, and the bill is the frequency charge plus pounds times the per-100-lb rate. DSNY rollout page: sign-up in Brooklyn North and Upper Manhattan from October 1 to November 30, 2026; Brooklyn East and Manhattan Northeast from January 1 to March 1, 2027; Manhattan West and Queens West from April 1 to June 1, 2027. A worked example (my arithmetic, zone rates per 100 lb not seen): 40 lb a day x 30 = 1,200 lb x $17.64 / 100 = $212, plus $110 = $322 a month in Brooklyn North at the caps, against the pack's $250.

suppliers.what: Milk, plant milk, syrups, cups, pastry and coffee from many brands on one order, restocked overnight inside the shop
suppliers.whereToFind: Search for cafe supply distributors that serve your borough; the service starts with a site visit to set up overnight access. Compare its prices line by line with your current invoices before you move everything.
suppliers.priceAnchor: No delivery fee; the company claims an average 20% saving on cost of goods (its own figure)
suppliers.minimumOrder: Advertised as none; an older FAQ says minimums may apply
suppliers.leadTime: Order in the morning, stocked overnight; most orders within one to two business days
suppliers.failureModes: One supplier means one point of failure; a driver needs a key or a code to your shop at 3 am
suppliers.note: Read through search summaries of Odeko's own pages and Barista Magazine: nightly delivery with no minimum and no delivery charge, supply concentrated in New York City, software that reads the POS and suggests the order. The 20% is a company claim, not an independent figure. One company is named because it is the best-known of its kind in New York, not as an endorsement.

suppliers.what: Dairy, produce, bread, dry goods and paper by truck, six days a week
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the restaurants on your block whose truck stops there. Ask for the minimum for your address and the cutoff for next-day delivery, and read the invoice for fuel and congestion surcharges.
suppliers.examples: Baldor Specialty Foods, The Chefs' Warehouse (Dairyland), Sysco, US Foods
suppliers.priceAnchor: No delivery fee above the minimum; in Manhattan below 60th Street suppliers add $1 to $10 per delivery for the congestion toll
suppliers.minimumOrder: $200-$500 an order by distance at one specialty distributor; a national broadliner advertises no minimum on its next-day service
suppliers.paymentTerms: Cash on delivery or card until a credit application clears, then weekly or net 14-30, usually with the owner's personal guarantee
suppliers.leadTime: Order by 8-10 pm for the next day
suppliers.failureModes: A small cafe struggles to fill a $350 order twice a week without overbuying perishables; in a shortage distributors serve their biggest accounts first
suppliers.note: Read through search: Baldor help center (minimums $200, $350, $500 from the Bronx warehouse; no delivery fee for business accounts); US Foods next-day page (no minimum, order by 8 pm, six-day delivery); 2025 press on congestion pricing (suppliers adding $1 to $10 per delivery; a distributor group of 200 firms asked for an exemption); a forum post from a 2021-2022 shortage in which a distributor said it could fully serve only its top 31% of accounts. Credit terms are trade practice.

suppliers.what: Walk in, load a cart, pay, drive it back: milk, oat milk, syrups, cups, cleaning supplies, with no minimum and no delivery fee
suppliers.whereToFind: Membership is free: bring your business license or the tax ID letter. Warehouses sit in Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx, so every trip costs fuel, parking, tolls and two to three hours.
suppliers.leadTime: Same day, in your own car
suppliers.failureModes: The owner is off the floor for half a day a week; the cold chain between the warehouse and your fridge is your responsibility; in 2026 the chain agreed to be bought by Sysco, and terms may change
suppliers.note: Restaurant Depot's membership page (through search): free membership on proof of business ownership (business license or IRS letter), no minimum purchase. Trade press in October 2026 reported Sysco's pending acquisition of Jetro Restaurant Depot; I did not check the deal's status.

suppliers.what: Shelf-stable barista cartons by the case; they need a fridge only after opening
suppliers.whereToFind: Your cafe distributor, a cash-and-carry warehouse or online by the case. Keep four weeks on the shelf: it does not spoil unopened, and shortages come without warning.
suppliers.examples: Oatly Barista Edition, Pacific Foods Barista Series, Minor Figures, Elmhurst, Califia
suppliers.priceAnchor: $39.99 per case of twelve 32 oz cartons: 10.4 cents an ounce against 4.1 for dairy
suppliers.failureModes: The market leader ran short in 2021 and was part of a 53-product recall in 2022; it announced US price increases for 2027; switching brands changes how the milk steams and how regulars' drinks taste
suppliers.monthlyVolume: About 188 cartons (16 cases) at 6,000 orders a month
suppliers.note: WebstaurantStore: Oatly Barista Edition $39.99 per case of 12 (lots of 85 cases: $35.49). Through search: Starbucks ran out of oat milk in April 2021, a month after its national launch; Lyons Magnus recalled 53 products including Oatly Barista Edition sold to foodservice in 2022; trade press of November 2, 2026: Oatly will raise US prices in 2027 to offset diesel costs.

suppliers.category: Syrups, sauces, chai, tea and matcha
suppliers.what: Flavoring syrups, chocolate sauce, chai concentrate, tea bags, matcha powder
suppliers.whereToFind: Online by the case or through your cafe distributor. For matcha, ask the importer about purchase limits and how long today's price holds.
suppliers.examples: Monin, Torani, Ghirardelli, Tazo, Oregon Chai, David Rio, Harney & Sons, Jade Leaf, Ippodo, Sugimoto
suppliers.priceAnchor: Syrup $84.99 per case of twelve 750 mL bottles (21 cents a drink); chocolate sauce $118.49 per case of six 64 oz jugs; chai $35.49 per case of six cartons; barista matcha $139.83 per lb (92 cents a drink)
suppliers.minimumOrder: One bottle; cases are 20-30% cheaper per unit
suppliers.leadTime: Two to five days; matcha from Japan one to six months when supply is tight
suppliers.failureModes: Matcha: purchase limits and waits that grew from one or two months to six in 2025; seasonal syrups bought in September are dead stock in January
suppliers.note: All four prices seen at WebstaurantStore (see extra.ingredients). Matcha waits and purchase limits: Supply Chain Dive, 2025, through search.

suppliers.category: Frozen pastry to bake in the shop
suppliers.what: Ready-to-bake croissants, proof-and-bake dough, muffin batter, cookie dough
suppliers.whereToFind: Online restaurant suppliers and broadline distributors. You need a freezer, an oven and someone who starts baking 40 minutes before the doors open.
suppliers.examples: Bridor, LeCoq Cuisine, Orange Bakery, Schulstad, Pillsbury
suppliers.priceAnchor: $1.37 per ready-to-bake croissant ($109.99 per case of 80); raw dough that needs proofing $0.71 ($113.99 per case of 160)
suppliers.minimumOrder: One case; frozen freight is charged separately
suppliers.leadTime: Three to seven days; a case lasts about a week
suppliers.failureModes: A freezer failure loses the whole stock; a croissant baked from frozen is good, not great, and regulars can tell
suppliers.note: WebstaurantStore: Bridor ready-to-bake croissant 2.8 oz 80/case $109.99 ($72.99 for paying members); Bridor raw butter croissant 160/case $113.99; Orange Bakery almond croissant 80/case $96.99; Pillsbury freezer-to-oven dough 100/case $77.37.

suppliers.what: Stock cups printed with your logo
suppliers.whereToFind: Specialist printers quote by the case. Start with one-case minimums; move to pallet runs only when your logo, cup sizes and volume have stopped changing.
suppliers.examples: Your Brand Cafe, Good Start Packaging, Morrison Cup Solutions, LogoCup
suppliers.priceAnchor: Quote only; expect a few cents a cup above stock at small runs
suppliers.minimumOrder: From one case of 500-1,000 at one printer to 50 cases or 30,000 cups at others
suppliers.leadTime: 3-4 weeks at the small-run printer; 12-19 weeks for big runs
suppliers.failureModes: Cash and storage tied up for months; reorder late and you are back to plain cups; change the logo and the stock is waste
suppliers.note: Read through search summaries of the printers' own pages: Your Brand Cafe (one case of 500-1,000; 3-4 weeks), Good Start Packaging (from 50 cases; 14-19 weeks), Morrison (30,000 paper cups; 12 weeks), LogoCup (50 cups; about 10 days). No per-cup price was published.

suppliers.category: Selling or giving away what is left at closing
suppliers.what: A surplus-food app that sells end-of-day bags at a third of the shelf price, or a food rescue group that collects donations
suppliers.whereToFind: Sign up on the app's business page; set the number of bags each afternoon once you see what is left. For donation, call a food rescue group that picks up small quantities.
suppliers.examples: Too Good To Go; City Harvest; Rescuing Leftover Cuisine
suppliers.priceAnchor: The app keeps an annual fee and a fee per bag (about a quarter of the bag price in the only US figure found); donation is free
suppliers.failureModes: Staff start over-ordering because 'the app will take it'; bag buyers arrive in the last busy half hour
suppliers.note: Read through search: Too Good To Go's business page (free to join, annual fee plus a fee per bag sold, the partner sets the bag price) and a 2023 San Diego Union-Tribune report (fee about 25%); payouts quarterly. Food rescue names are well-known New York groups from general knowledge, not checked in this session.

suppliers.what: Hand-rolled bagels and rolls from a route bakery, delivered before opening
suppliers.whereToFind: Ask the delis and cafes nearby who delivers their bagels: route bakeries rarely advertise. Shipped wholesale boxes exist but are meant to be frozen.
suppliers.examples: Local route bagel bakeries; New Yorker Bagels for shipped boxes
suppliers.priceAnchor: About $1.17 a bagel shipped (12 dozen for $169); cream cheese about $3.99 per lb in a 30 lb case
suppliers.minimumOrder: By the dozen on a route; 6 dozen for shipped boxes
suppliers.paymentTerms: Weekly invoice or cash to the driver
suppliers.leadTime: Nightly on a route; two days shipped
suppliers.failureModes: Not shipped or delivered on major holidays; in December 2021 New York bagel shops could not buy cream cheese for weeks
suppliers.note: Read through search: New Yorker Bagels wholesale pages (12 dozen for $169 shipped; tiers from 6 to 72 dozen; not shipped on major holidays; a wholesale account is required); Foodomarket New York quote for cream cheese, June 1, 2026; NY1 and the New York Times on the December 2021 cream cheese shortage.

suppliers.what: Cases of bottled drinks for the grab-and-go fridge
suppliers.whereToFind: A beverage distributor or the cash-and-carry warehouse. The distributor charges you the 5-cent deposit on each bottle; you charge it to the customer and refund it on empties.
suppliers.priceAnchor: About 40 cents a bottle of water by the case (not checked), sold for $3
suppliers.failureModes: Selling deposit bottles makes you a 'dealer': anyone may bring you up to 240 empties a day of the brands you sell, and you need the signs and somewhere to keep the bags
suppliers.note: NYS DEC dealer requirements: refunds in all business hours except the first and last for a shop open less than 24 hours; containers of the brand, size and shape the dealer sells, wherever bought; a dealer may limit returns to no fewer than 240 containers per person a day if it posts the limit; the 'Redemption Warning' and 'Bottle Bill of Rights' signs are required.
